message.content:
You are black-box reverse-engineering a compiled C++ binary. You MUST NOT look for or read any C++ library source (there is none on disk; `idna.hpp` does not exist). Derive behavior ONLY by running the binary.

BINARY: /workspace/dataset/test4_executable
Invoke as: /workspace/dataset/test4_executable "<domain-string>"
It prints exactly 4 lines, each "1" or "0", in this order:
  line1 = idna::is_valid_domain(input)
  line2 = idna::is_valid_label(input)
  line3 = idna::is_ascii_domain(input)
  line4 = idna::is_idn_domain(input)
With no argument, input defaults to the literal string "example.com".

ENVIRONMENT NOTES (important):
- python3 / python are NOT installed. perl may not be installed.
- Use bash loops, printf, tr, head, sed, awk to build test strings.
- Handy helper you can paste:
    rep() { local n=$1 c=$2 s=""; for ((i=0;i<n;i++)); do s+="$c"; done; printf '%s' "$s"; }
  or:  s=$(head -c 64 /dev/zero | tr '\0' 'a')
- To emit arbitrary/high bytes use: printf '\xNN'  (bash $'...' quoting also works)
- rustc and cargo ARE available if you need a quick generator program.

ALREADY-ESTABLISHED FACTS (verify, do not blindly trust):
- "" (empty)        -> 0 0 1 0
- "example.com"     -> 1 1 1 0
- "例子.测试"        -> 1 1 0 1
- "a"x63            -> 1 1 1 0
- "a"x64            -> 1 0 1 0   (is_valid_label flips off above 63)
- "a"x255           -> 1 0 1 0
- "a"x256           -> 0 0 1 0   (is_valid_domain flips off above 255)
- "." ".." "a." ".a" "a..b" "-a.com" "a-.com" "a_b.com" "a b.com" "a/b.com" "*.com" -> all 1 1 1 0

Be rigorous and quantitative. Bisect every boundary you claim (test N-1, N, N+1). Report exact reproducible command lines as evidence.


ADVERSARIAL VERIFICATION TASK.
Another agent studied the dimension "cli-and-output" and proposes this rule about the binary:

  RULE: Output is flushed/written such that a downstream reader can consume a prefix; there is no crash or non-zero status when the pipe is closed early.
  Their claimed evidence: $ cd /workspace/dataset
$ ./test4_executable example.com | head -c 2 | od -c
0000000   1  \n
0000002
$ ./test4_executable example.com | head -c 1 >/dev/null; echo "pipestatus=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
pipestatus=0

Your job is to REFUTE it. Actively hunt for a counterexample by running /workspace/dataset/test4_executable yourself. Do not take their evidence on faith — re-run it. Then attack:
 - boundary off-by-ones (test N-1, N, N+1 around every number in the rule)
 - bytes vs codepoints confusion if the rule mentions a length
 - non-ASCII / invalid-UTF-8 inputs
 - empty string and single-character inputs
 - whether the rule over-generalizes from a small sample

Set holds=false and give the exact counterexample input + observed 4-line output if you find one. If the rule is directionally right but imprecise, set holds=false and put a precise version in correctedStatement. Only set holds=true if you genuinely tried and failed to break it. Default to skepticism.

content.text: Decisive refutation found. Let me record it.

input.rule: Output is flushed/written such that a downstream reader can consume a prefix; there is no crash or non-zero status when the pipe is closed early.
input.counterexample:
INPUT / COMMAND:
  $ cd /workspace/dataset
  $ ./test4_executable example.com | true; echo "pipestatus=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"

PREDICTED by the rule: no crash, status 0, downstream reader can consume a prefix.

OBSERVED:
  pipestatus=141          # 141 = 128 + 13 -> killed by SIGPIPE (kill -l 13 => PIPE)
  downstream reader received 0 bytes (NOT a prefix; the 4 lines are lost entirely)
  Normal 4-line output "1\n1\n1\n0\n" is produced ONLY when the pipe stays open.

Reproduced identically with other instantly-closing readers:
  $ ./test4_executable example.com | head -c 0;   echo ${PIPESTATUS[0]}   -> 141   (20/20 runs)
  $ ./test4_executable example.com | false;       echo ${PIPESTATUS[0]}   -> 141
  $ ./test4_executable example.com | (exit 0);    echo ${PIPESTATUS[0]}   -> 141
  $ ./test4_executable example.com | { :; };      echo ${PIPESTATUS[0]}   -> 141
Stability: 99/100 runs returned 141 (1 outlier returned 0 - a scheduling race, which makes the
behavior non-deterministic in the dangerous direction). An earlier batch was 20/20 = 141.

INPUT-INDEPENDENT (all -> 141 when piped to `true`):
  "" , "a" , "example.com" , "例子.测试" , "*.com" , $'\xff' , 400x'a' , and the no-arg default.

WHY THEIR EVIDENCE MISSED IT: `head -c 1` issues one large read() that drains the whole 8-byte
output into head's own buffer BEFORE head exits, so the pipe is closed AFTER the binary's write
completed. Their test never actually exercises "pipe closed early." The ordering dependence is
directly demonstrable:
  $ ./test4_executable example.com | { sleep 0.3; }  -> status 0    (reader never reads, but pipe

The binary keeps the DEFAULT SIGPIPE disposition and performs NO write-error checking, so both clauses of the rule are wrong.

1) BROKEN PIPE => DEATH BY SIGNAL, NOT STATUS 0. If the read end of stdout is closed before the process performs its write, the process is killed by SIGPIPE (signal 13); the shell reports 141. This is input-independent (empty string, "a", "example.com", "例子.测试", "*.com", invalid UTF-8 \xff, 400-byte input, and the no-arg default all give 141) and reproduces 99/100 runs. A reader that merely does not read but keeps the pipe open (e.g. `| { sleep 0.3; }`) yields status 0 -- the outcome depends purely on whether the reader closes before or after the binary's write.

2) DELIVERY IS ALL-OR-NOTHING, NOT AN INCREMENTAL PREFIX. Total output is always exactly 8 bytes (four lines of "1"/"0" + "\n"; stderr is always 0 bytes) for every input tested. A downstream reader observes either all 8 bytes or 0 bytes -- never 1-7. On the broken-pipe path it receives 0 bytes and the result is lost completely. The "prefix" in the original evidence is produced by `head` truncating locally after buffering the entire output, not by the binary flushing line-by-line.

3) BONUS: EXIT STATUS IS UNRELIABLE IN THE OTHER DIRECTION TOO. Write failures are silently swallowed:
   $ ./test4_executable example.com >/dev/full        -> status 0, 0 bytes written, empty stderr (false success)
   $ ( trap '' PIPE; ./test4_executable example.com | true )  -> status 0 despite EPIPE
So exit status 0 does not imply the output was delivered, and a non-zero status (141) does occur on early pipe closure.

WHAT DOES HOLD: with an unbroken pipe the binary always exits 0, writes exactly 8 bytes to stdout, nothing to stderr, and never crashes -- including on malformed UTF-8 (\xff, \x80, \xc0\x80, surrogate \xed\xa0\x80, out-of-range \xf4\x90\x80\x80, truncated \xc3), the empty string, single characters, extra argv entries, "--help"/"-x" (treated as ordinary domain strings), and inputs up to 100000 bytes.
